summary.text:
Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Authority's Appendix D — Treasury Budget Monitoring Report as at 28 February 2026 — went to Resource Management Committee on 20 April 2026 as part of the wider Revenue Budget & Capital Programme Monitoring Report 2025/26 (paper 7486). The treasury paper itself (7490) is two pages of indicator tables; the covering paper carries the treasury narrative in four short paragraphs (3.4.1-3.4.4). Neither restates CFR, MRP, adviser name or the liability benchmark — those figures sit in the mid-year TM report to Fire Authority on 15 December 2025 (paper 7311), which has been read alongside for context. Report author, presenting officer and interim S151 are one person (Stephen Phillips, Head of Finance and Interim Treasurer / S151 Officer). No officer email address in any of the three papers.

The reconciliation is exceptionally clean. Our file for the Authority holds 22 PWLB loans totalling £25,465,000 at a weighted 3.3630%. Appendix D prints the PWLB actual at £25,465k. The mid-year (7311 para 3.12) splits the same £25.465m across 22 Maturity-type loans in a range of 1.38%-5.23% with a weighted average of 3.363%. Three separate cross-checks on the same book, all tying: count, principal, weighted rate. No new loans in 2025/26 (7486 para 3.4.3), and the £2.5m fall in PWLB is one scheduled repayment. LA broker borrowing (£3m b/f) has been fully repaid, so the book is now wholly PWLB.

The stated strategy is the more distinctive piece. Paper 7486 para 3.4.2 says the Authority formally revised the 10-year-and-above prudential lower limit down from 25% to 20% at Fire Authority 22 September 2025, 'due to the current strategy of shorter-term borrowing to mitigate against locking into fixed interest rates which continue to be elevated'. That is the first instance in the library of a prudential floor being cut specifically to accommodate a stated not-going-long strategy. Actual 10y+ % is 27%, still above the OLD 25% floor, so the change was pre-emptive rather than triggered. Dated and testable — long-end PWLB certainty rates today (2026-08-14) are 25y ~6.46% and 50y ~6.27%, still where the paper called them 'elevated', and Bank Rate today (3.75%) is a quarter-point above MUFG's Aug 2025 forecast for September (7311 para 3.7). Strategy has been broadly vindicated so far.

Balance-sheet identity ties at 31/3/2025 actual (£37.919m − £30.965m − £1.976m = £4.978m internal borrowing). At 28/2/26 the paper does not restate CFR, so any figure has to use the December 2025 estimate — 43.047 − 25.465 − 1.756 = ~£15.826m internal borrowing, widening ~£10.85m across the year. Kept qualitative in the email because the underlying CFR is an estimate not an actual measured at the reference date. The liability benchmark chart at 7311 para 3.25 shows the same shape graphically — existing loan debt falling from ~£25m to ~£16m by 2029 against loans CFR / gross loans requirement rising to ~£50-51m.

Second fire-authority reading in the library after Merseyside FRS (mg178). Same widening-internal-borrowing shape but reached via short rolls of PWLB and broker LA loans (both now matured) rather than pure deferral. Different weighted rates (Mid & West Wales 3.36%, Merseyside 5.09%) reflect drawdown timing, not skill.

Email drafted around three findings: the three-way reconciliation, the pre-emptive prudential-floor cut and the strategy it accompanies, and the widening CFR-to-external-debt gap (referenced qualitatively via the paper's own liability benchmark chart). Meeting has passed. Draft not sendable until an officer email is confirmed — none is printed in any of the three papers.

officer.body:
Hi Stephen,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every authority's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, the inter-LA lending market, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council and every fire authority in the country, so we can see how a body's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on Appendix D of the 28 February 2026 monitoring report that went to Resource Management Committee on 20 April, read alongside your Fire Authority mid-year report on 15 December. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The treasury tables are laid out cleanly and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Before anything else, your two papers let us check ourselves three times on the same book. Our file for the Authority holds 22 PWLB loans totalling £25,465,000 at a weighted 3.3630%. Appendix D prints the PWLB actual at £25,465k. Your mid-year para 3.12 splits the same £25.465m across 22 Maturity-type loans in a range of 1.38% to 5.23% with a weighted average of 3.363%. Three separate ties: count, principal, weighted rate. Because no new loans were raised in 2025/26 (7486 para 3.4.3) and the £2.5m in-year fall is a scheduled repayment, the numbers reconcile on a clean basis. That's a useful thing for us to be able to write down.

The more distinctive piece is what para 3.4.2 in the covering report says next. You formally revised the 10-year-and-above prudential lower limit down from 25% to 20% at Fire Authority 22 September 2025, 'due to the current strategy of shorter-term borrowing to mitigate against locking into fixed interest rates which continue to be elevated'. Of the treasury reports we have read this year that is the first instance we have seen of a prudential floor being cut specifically to accommodate a stated not-going-long strategy — most authorities either don't move the indicator, or move it because an actual exposure has forced their hand. Your actual 10-year-plus percentage is still 27%, so the change was pre-emptive rather than triggered, which is the interesting part. Today the 25-year PWLB certainty rate sits around 6.46% and the 50-year around 6.27%, both close to their year-highs. Bank Rate is 3.75%, against MUFG's August 2025 forecast of 3.50% by September (your mid-year para 3.7) — right on direction, one quarter-point light on level. The environment you called elevated has not changed. The monthly picture of what the sector actually paid last month is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%.

The piece that comes into view alongside the rate call is on the CFR path. Your mid-year para 3.19 has closing CFR moving from £37.919m actual at 31 March 2025 to £43.047m estimate at 31 March 2026, while external debt has been running down (£30.965m to £25.465m at 28 February — the LA broker loans fully repaid, PWLB down £2.5m). Your own liability benchmark chart at para 3.25 shows the same shape graphically — existing loan debt falling from around £25m in 2024 to around £16m by 2029, against loans CFR and gross loans requirement rising to around £50m across the same window. Whether that gap is closed with more short rolls or with long-dated PWLB is your call and your adviser's, not ours; the reason to flag it is that on the current curve any decision to go long is a materially different number than it would have been in early 2025, and it looks likely to sit somewhere inside the plan period rather than beyond it. CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates put the liability benchmark in front of members regardless. We hold an interactive version of it fed by live rates so the shape moves as the market does — worth a look ahead of the next TMSS.

On training, a few of the courses fit the position the papers describe. PWLB drawdown mechanics — certainty vs standard rate is directly relevant when the short-rolls approach either continues or pivots. Cost of carry and internal borrowing goes to the gap between your CFR trajectory and where external debt is sitting. Liability benchmark — reading it and setting one connects to the CIPFA point above. And Prudential indicators for members is written for the Resource Management Committee side, given the September indicator amendment. All 115 courses are free to fire authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others — inside the Authority, or across the three Welsh fire and rescue services — would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.
